  - Appellate Motions for Rehearing Generally In Florida’s state appellate courts, motions for rehearing are governed by Fla. R. App. P. 9.330. Rule 9.330 sets forth the time for filing a motion for rehearing, as well as the required contents and available grounds for such a motion. The following discussion will address each of these elements. Motions for rehearing en banc will also be discussed, as well as the potential for sanctions for failure to comply with the applicable rules.
[...]
• Contents of the Motion — Rule 9.330 sets forth the necessary contents for a rehearing motion as follows: “A motion for rehearing shall state with particularity the points of law or fact that, in the opinion of the movant, the court has overlooked or misapprehended in its decision, and shall not present issues not previously raised in the proceeding.”6 Thus, the motion must state the particular factual or legal basis for the rehearing. It must not contain new issues, and it must avoid rearguing the merits of the appellate court’s decision.7
[...]
• Grounds for the Motion — The required contents of a rehearing motion are directly related to the available grounds for the motion. In short, the grounds for rehearing are limited to points of law and fact the court misapprehended or overlooked in its original decision. The reason for the limited grounds available is rooted in the limited purpose of rehearing.
[...]
Rehearing is not a forum for expressing disagreement with the appellate court’s decision,8 nor is it an opportunity to interject new issues or evidence not previously considered in the proceedings.9 Moreover, a rehearing is not a reconsideration. The language of Rule 9.330 does not authorize a motion that attempts to reargue issues already considered and determined by the appellate court.10 Rather, the motion must be based on specific points of law or fact that the appellate court “overlooked” or “misapprehended” in its decision.11 The purpose of rehearing is solely to correct these types of errors. Thus, a proper motion for rehearing is demonstrative and contains only limited argument. In other words, it points out to the appellate court an issue of fact or law that it “missed” in making its decision. Although easily stated, this distinction can be tricky in practice (and even trickier to explain to your client).
[...]
Advisability of Filing the Motion The foregoing demonstrates the strict requirements of Rule 9.330 governing rehearing. Rehearing will be granted rarely and only when the limited grounds set forth by the rule are presented and established.14 A motion for rehearing should have a reasonable chance of success if the moving party can identify a critical fact the court overlooked or misunderstood in reaching its original decision, or if the moving party can direct the court’s attention to a recent or controlling statute or case the court may have overlooked.15 An appellate court’s decision to grant a rehearing is generally based on something that was missed by the appellate court — not by the attorneys or parties — in determining its original opinion. However, there will likely be few cases in which the appellate court actually “overlooks” critical record evidence or “misapprehends” a point of law. Thus, there are likely few cases in which a motion for rehearing will be granted. This should not discourage attorneys from filing a motion for rehearing if the appropriate grounds exist, but it certainly should be kept in mind when discussing with a client the advisability of filing a motion for rehearing.

5. Florida Motion for Rehearing: What You Need to Know - LegalClarity
   URL: https://legalclarity.org/florida-motion-for-rehearing-what-you-need-to-know/
   Highlights:
  - A motion for rehearing is a formal request asking a judge to reconsider and change a final order or judgment they have just made. Its purpose is to point out a significant error of law or fact that the court may have overlooked or misunderstood, giving the judge a chance to correct the mistake without needing to file an appeal. This is not an opportunity to present new evidence that was previously available, introduce new legal theories, or simply re-argue points the court has already considered and rejected.
[...]
A motion for rehearing is not granted lightly and must be based on specific, recognized grounds. You cannot file one simply because you are unhappy with the outcome of your case. These motions are governed by procedural rules like the Florida Rules of Civil Procedure.
[...]
One of the most common grounds is that the court overlooked a controlling statute or a binding court precedent. For example, if a judge’s ruling in a contract dispute directly contradicts a specific Florida statute that governs the type of contract in question, a motion for rehearing would be appropriate to bring that statute to the court’s attention.
[...]
Another basis for rehearing is that the court misapprehended a key fact that was already part of the official case record. For instance, if a final judgment in a family law case states the marital home was purchased in 2015, but bank records in evidence clearly show it was purchased in 2010, a motion could be filed to correct this factual error.
[...]
When preparing a motion for rehearing, the content must be precise and focused. The document should begin with a clear title, such as “Plaintiff’s Motion for Rehearing,” to identify its purpose. The first paragraph must state the specific final judgment or order you are asking the court to reconsider, including the date it was filed.
[...]
The core of the motion is the argument, which must state with “particularity” the specific points of law or fact the court overlooked or misapprehended. This means you cannot be vague. You must pinpoint the exact legal precedent, statute, or piece of evidence from the record that you believe was wrongly applied or ignored. For example, you would cite the specific case law you believe is controlling or reference an exhibit number or transcript page to show a factual error. An effective motion focuses solely on the mistake and explains why correcting it would lead to a different result.

                  STATE OF FLORIDA / LEE COUNTY'S MOTION FOR REHEARING

        Plaintiff, the State of Florida, by and through the Office of the Lee County Attorney, pursuant to Florida Rule of Civil Procedure 1.530(a)–(d), respectfully moves this Court for rehearing of its Order of Dismissal entered July 2, 2025 (the "Order"), and as grounds therefor states:

                                    I. INTRODUCTION

        1. On April 10, 2025, Lee County Park Ranger Shannon Coyle issued Defendant a citation under Lee County Ordinance No. 18-12, § 4.9, for unlicensed concession/vending on Lee County park property at Dog Beach Park.

        2. On June 25, 2025, the Court conducted a non-jury hearing on the citation. At the close of the hearing, the Court reserved ruling on the Defendant's then-pending Motion to Dismiss.

        3. On July 2, 2025, the Court entered the Order, granting Defendant's Motion to Dismiss and dismissing the citation.

        4. The County respectfully submits that the Order overlooks or misapprehends material points of fact in the record and material points of controlling Florida law, and that those errors—if corrected—would compel a different result. See Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.530(a); Pingree v. Quaintance, 394 So. 2d 161, 162 (Fla. 1st DCA 1981) ("The purpose of a motion for rehearing is to give the trial court an opportunity to consider matters which it overlooked or failed to consider, and to correct any error if it becomes convinced that it has erred."); Frieman v. Frieman, 953 So. 2d 619, 619–20 (Fla. 4th DCA 2007).

                                  II. STANDARD OF REVIEW

        5. A motion for rehearing under Rule 1.530(a) is the proper procedural vehicle by which a party may direct the trial court's attention to matters of fact in the record or matters of law that were "overlooked or misapprehended" in the dispositive order. See Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.530(a); Pingree, 394 So. 2d at 162. The motion is timely if served within fifteen (15) days of the filing of the judgment or final order in a non-jury action. Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.530(b). The Order was filed July 2, 2025; this motion is timely served and filed.

        6. On a motion for rehearing of a matter heard without a jury, the Court "may open the judgment if one has been entered, take additional testimony, and enter a new judgment." Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.530(a).

                                       III. ARGUMENT

A. THE COURT OVERLOOKED UNREBUTTED RECORD EVIDENCE THAT DEFENDANT'S VESSEL WAS PHYSICALLY ON THE DRY-SAND PORTION OF DOG BEACH PARK AT THE TIME OF THE OFFENSE.

        7. The Order finds that "[i]t was clear from the testimony that defendant was outside the 'mean high-water line' and, ergo, on State property." Order at 1. That finding overlooks the unrebutted, sworn testimony of Park Ranger Shannon Coyle—corroborated by the photograph admitted as the Court's Exhibit A (filed June 13, 2025)—that "the front three feet of [Defendant's] boat is on dry sand," with the remainder of the vessel astern in the littoral water. Tr. 8:18–19; see also Tr. 12:4–9 ("not only is the front of his boat on dry sand, the back of his boat is still within littoral waters."). Defendant did not contradict that testimony at hearing; to the contrary, on cross-examination Ranger Coyle reiterated that "[t]he front of his boat, however, was dry and anybody that was getting food did not have to step in the water to get his food." Tr. 21:23–25.

        8. The Court's Exhibit A photograph, admitted without objection, depicts the bow of the vessel resting on dry sand. Tr. 9:10 ("I have no objection to the photograph, Judge."). That admitted physical evidence was overlooked in the Order's finding that the entire vessel was seaward of the mean high-water line.

        9. Because the Defendant's vessel was, in fact, partially situated on the dry sand of Dog Beach Park—indisputably above any mean high-water line and unambiguously on Lee County park property—the predicate factual finding of the Order is contrary to the record. See Fla. Stat. § 177.27(15) (2024) (defining "mean high-water line" as the intersection of the tidal plane of mean high water with the shore). Lee County Ordinance No. 18-12 expressly prohibits the operation of "any . . . vessel for the . . . sale . . . of any . . . article" on park property without a written permit. Lee County, Fla., Ordinance No. 18-12, § 4.9. The portion of Defendant's vessel actually grounded on park sand was a "vessel" stationed on "park property" within the meaning of the Ordinance; the citation should not have been dismissed on the assumption to the contrary.

B. THE COURT OVERLOOKED THE INDEPENDENT FACT THAT DEFENDANT'S VENDING TRANSACTIONS OCCURRED ON THE DRY-SAND PORTION OF THE PARK.

        10. Even if the vessel itself were entirely seaward of the mean high-water line (which the record refutes), the Court overlooked the unrebutted testimony that the prohibited sales activity—the actus reus of § 4.9—was directed to and conducted with patrons standing on the County park's dry sand. Ranger Coyle testified that "there were people purchasing food off his boat" (Tr. 7:20–21) and that "anybody that was getting food did not have to step in the water to get his food" (Tr. 21:24–25). Section 4.9 reaches not only the placement of a "vessel" but also any "person" who "expose[s] or offer[s] for sale any . . . article" on park property. Lee County Ordinance No. 18-12, § 4.9. The vending transactions plainly occurred at the boundary between the bow of the vessel and the dry sand of Dog Beach Park—on the County's land, not in sovereignty submerged waters.

C. THE COURT MISAPPREHENDED THE SCOPE AND HOLDING OF STOP THE BEACH RENOURISHMENT, INC. v. FLORIDA DEPARTMENT OF ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION.

        11. The Order rests its dismissal on the Court's reading of Stop the Beach Renourishment, Inc. v. Florida Department of Environmental Protection, 560 U.S. 702 (2010). See Order at 1. Stop the Beach addressed only whether a state-court determination concerning the boundary between privately owned uplands and state-owned submerged lands effected a judicial taking under the Fifth Amendment. Id. at 715–17 (plurality op.). It did not concern—and does not control—the entirely distinct question of whether a county may regulate commercial vending on its own park property under its home-rule and police powers. To extend Stop the Beach to bar enforcement of a county park ordinance against a vendor whose vessel is partially grounded on county park sand and whose patrons are standing on county park sand misapprehends the holding.

        12. The cited Florida Supreme Court precedent—Broward v. Mabry, 58 Fla. 398, 50 So. 826 (1909)—likewise does not support dismissal. Mabry holds that the State takes title to the beds of navigable waters in trust for "navigation, commerce, fishing, bathing, and other easements allowed by law." 50 So. at 829–30. The trust was not created for the benefit of a private vendor seeking to convert sovereignty submerged land into his personal commercial premises; nor does Mabry preempt local police-power regulation of conduct occurring on adjacent uplands held by a county.

D. THE COURT OVERLOOKED LEE COUNTY'S CONSTITUTIONAL AND STATUTORY HOME-RULE AUTHORITY OVER ITS OWN PARK PROPERTY.

        13. Article VIII, section 1(g) of the Florida Constitution and Florida Statutes section 125.01(1) confer broad home-rule authority on Lee County, including the power to "[a]dopt, by reference or in full, and enforce . . . county ordinances," Fla. Stat. § 125.01(1)(t) (2024), and to regulate "the use of property . . . for purposes of public health, safety, and welfare," id. § 125.01(1)(h). The Order does not address—and therefore overlooks—the threshold proposition that the County is the fee owner and operator of Dog Beach Park (see Lee County Ordinance No. 18-12, § 3.1), with full authority to license and regulate vending occurring on its own park property.

E. THE COURT OVERLOOKED THAT THE PUBLIC TRUST DOCTRINE PROTECTS PUBLIC USE—NOT PRIVATE COMMERCIAL VENDING.

        14. The public-trust uses recognized by Florida law are "navigation, commerce, fishing, bathing, and other easements allowed by law." Broward v. Mabry, 50 So. 826, 830 (Fla. 1909); Fla. Const. art. X, § 11. The "commerce" referenced in the public trust is general public navigation and shipping for the benefit of all Floridians—it is not a private right vested in a single vendor to operate an unlicensed commercial enterprise from sovereignty submerged lands. Defendant's argument inverts the doctrine: he claims a private right to monopolize a portion of the foreshore for his own commercial purposes free of regulation. The Order's adoption of that inversion overlooks the controlling, public-purpose construction of the public-trust doctrine.

F. THE COURT MISAPPREHENDED FLORIDA STATUTE § 177.27(14)–(15).

        15. The Order quotes Fla. Stat. § 177.27(14)–(15) as defining "mean high water" and "mean high-water line." Order at 1. Those subsections—part of the Coastal Mapping Act of 1974, Chapter 177, Part II—are surveying definitions used to fix property boundary lines for surveying and platting purposes; they do not displace the County's police-power authority to regulate vending on its parks, nor do they convert any portion of an upland park beach into State sovereignty land. Section 177.27 was not enacted to immunize commercial vendors from local park ordinances and was misapprehended in the Order to do exactly that.

                                      IV. CONCLUSION

        For the reasons above, the County respectfully requests that this Court (i) grant rehearing under Rule 1.530(a), (ii) vacate the Order of Dismissal entered July 2, 2025, (iii) reinstate the citation, and (iv) set the matter for further proceedings, including supplemental argument and—if the Court deems necessary—the receipt of additional testimony.

                    IN THE COUNTY COURT OF THE TWENTIETH JUDICIAL CIRCUIT
                              IN AND FOR LEE COUNTY, FLORIDA
                                       CIVIL ACTION

STATE OF FLORIDA,                                          CASE NO.: 25-CO-001864
        Plaintiff,
v.
CHARLES LEON LARSON,
        Defendant.

           PLAINTIFF'S RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO DEFENDANT'S MOTION TO DISMISS

        Plaintiff, the State of Florida (acting through the Office of the Lee County Attorney), files this Response in Opposition to Defendant's Motion to Dismiss and Incorporated Memorandum of Law (Filing # 224461849) and states:

                                 PRELIMINARY STATEMENT

        Defendant's Motion seeks to convert a routine ordinance-enforcement proceeding into a sweeping constitutional and preemption controversy, all to avoid responsibility for unlicensed commercial vending on Lee County park property. Each of the Motion's three pillars fails: (i) the unrebutted record evidence places Defendant's vessel and his vending transactions physically on the dry sand of Dog Beach Park, on County land; (ii) Florida's preemption statutes governing food-service licensing do not displace local authority to regulate where vending occurs on county-owned parks; and (iii) Defendant's bare assertion of "reliance" on unidentified County officials does not satisfy the rigorous standard for equitable estoppel against a governmental entity.

                                  FACTUAL BACKGROUND

        1. On April 10, 2025, Park Ranger Shannon Coyle observed Defendant operating a barbecue food-service vessel on Dog Beach Park, in Lee County, Florida. Tr. 7:11–22.

        2. Ranger Coyle testified, and Court's Exhibit A photographically depicts, that "the front three feet of [Defendant's] boat is on dry sand," with the stern in the littoral water. Tr. 8:18–19; Tr. 12:4–9. Patrons obtained food directly from the vessel without entering the water. Tr. 21:23–25.

        3. Ranger Coyle issued a citation pursuant to Lee County Ordinance No. 18-12, § 4.9, for operating a concession or vending service on park property without a written permit issued by the Board of County Commissioners or its designee. Tr. 6:16–18; 7:9–10; 12:7–9.

        4. Ranger Coyle further testified that Defendant had been warned on multiple prior occasions for the same conduct. Tr. 15:21–23 ("[H]e had been warned by me before not to do this, just not on county property. Not saying he can't sell; he just can't do it on county property.").

        5. Defendant testified that his business is operated from a Florida-DBPR-licensed mobile food-dispensing vessel, "Dark Knight Preservation." Tr. 23:8–14; 27:8–14; Def. Ex. 4.

                                       ARGUMENT

I.   THE CITATION RESTS ON CONDUCT OCCURRING ON LEE COUNTY PARK PROPERTY; THE COUNTY HAS UNCONTESTED HOME-RULE AUTHORITY TO REGULATE VENDING THERE.

A.   Defendant's Vessel and Sales Activity Were Physically Within the Park.

        Defendant's premise—that "Defendant's vessel was anchored and operating in navigable waters adjacent to Dog Beach . . . below the ordinary high-water mark," Mot. to Dismiss ¶ 2—is contradicted by his own evidentiary record. The unrebutted testimony of Ranger Coyle, corroborated by the admitted photograph (Court's Ex. A, June 13, 2025), establishes that the front three feet of the vessel were resting on the dry sand of Dog Beach Park. Tr. 8:18–19; 12:4–9. Defendant offered no testimony that his bow was below the mean high-water line; in fact, his own counsel did not dispute this when cross-examining the Ranger. Tr. 21:21–25.

        Section 4.9 of Lee County Ordinance No. 18-12 prohibits any "person" from "operat[ing] a concession or expos[ing] or offer[ing] for sale any service, article, or thing" or "stat[ing] or plac[ing] on park property any . . . vessel for the . . . sale . . . of any such article." Lee County, Fla., Ordinance No. 18-12, § 4.9. The ordinance defines "park" to include "beaches" and "abutting lands" of any park "operating and maintained by the Lee County Department of Parks and Recreation." Id. § 3.1. Defendant's vessel was, in part, "stationed or placed on park property" within the meaning of § 4.9; his sales were to patrons standing on the dry sand of Dog Beach Park, which by any measure is "on park property."

B.   The County's Home-Rule Authority Reaches Vending on County Parks.

        Lee County is a non-charter county vested with home-rule powers under Article VIII, section 1(f) of the Florida Constitution and Chapter 125, Florida Statutes. The Florida Supreme Court has confirmed that counties may exercise their police power "for any purpose not specifically prohibited by general or special law." Phantom of Brevard, Inc. v. Brevard County, 3 So. 3d 309, 314 (Fla. 2008). The legislature has expressly authorized counties to "[a]dopt, by reference or in full, and enforce . . . county ordinances," Fla. Stat. § 125.01(1)(t) (2024), and to regulate the use of "property" within their jurisdiction "for the purposes of protecting and preserving the public health, safety, and welfare," id. § 125.01(1)(h).

        A county's regulation of vending on park lands it owns and operates is a quintessential exercise of proprietary and police-power authority. See City of Daytona Beach v. Tona-Rama, Inc., 294 So. 2d 73, 78 (Fla. 1974) ("the right of the public of access to, and enjoyment of, Florida's oceans and beaches has long been recognized" and "is subject to appropriate governmental regulation"). Defendant's argument that the County loses jurisdiction the instant a vendor's stern floats over a sovereign water column would render every beach-side park in Florida a regulation-free zone for commercial enterprise. That is not the law.

C.   Broward v. Mabry Does Not Bar Enforcement.

        Defendant relies on Broward v. Mabry, 58 Fla. 398, 50 So. 826 (1909), for the unremarkable proposition that the State takes title to the beds of navigable waters in trust for the people. Mot. to Dismiss at 2. But Mabry is a title case, not a regulatory case. The Florida Supreme Court held that the State's trust is for "navigation, commerce, fishing, bathing, and other easements allowed by law." Mabry, 50 So. at 829–30. Those public-trust uses are uses by the public—not commercial monopolies by private operators. Mabry never held, and could not have held, that a private vendor acquires immunity from local ordinance enforcement merely by floating his commercial premises over sovereignty submerged lands.

        Indeed, Mabry expressly recognizes that public-trust uses remain "subject to lawful regulation by the States" (and, by extension, by their political subdivisions exercising delegated police power). Id. at 829–30. The Lee County ordinance does no more than that: it regulates commercial vending on County-controlled parks, leaving the navigation, fishing, and bathing rights of the general public unaffected.

II.  STATE LICENSURE OF DEFENDANT'S MOBILE FOOD-DISPENSING VESSEL DOES NOT PREEMPT LEE COUNTY'S VENDING-ON-PARKS ORDINANCE.

A.   Section 509.032(7), Florida Statutes, Preempts Only the Subjects Listed Therein.

        Defendant invokes Florida Statute § 509.032(7) (Mot. to Dismiss at 2), but the statute's text demonstrates that its preemption is narrow, not categorical. Subsection (7)(a) preempts "regulation of public lodging establishments and public food service establishments, including, but not limited to, sanitation standards, inspections, training and testing of personnel, and matters related to the nutritional content and marketing of foods." Fla. Stat. § 509.032(7)(a) (2024). The ordinance at issue here regulates none of those subjects. Section 4.9 of Ordinance 18-12 says nothing about food sanitation, food safety, employee training, nutritional content, or food marketing. It instead regulates the location and circumstances under which any "concession," "vending," or "peddling" may occur on County park property. That is a quintessential land-use and proprietary regulation, not a food-service regulation.

        Florida law is settled that an express preemption clause is read narrowly: "[w]hen the Legislature expressly preempts an area, the limits of preemption must be carefully evaluated." Sarasota All. for Fair Elections, Inc. v. Browning, 28 So. 3d 880, 886 (Fla. 2010); Phantom of Brevard, 3 So. 3d at 314 ("preemption need not be explicit so long as it is clear that the legislature has clearly preempted local regulation of the subject" — but the "subject" preempted is the subject specified). Section 509.032(7)(a) therefore does not bar a local park-vending ordinance.

B.   Section 509.102 Does Not Save Defendant Either.

        Section 509.102(2)(a), Florida Statutes, provides that "[r]egulation of mobile food dispensing vehicles . . . involving licenses, registrations, permits, and fees is preempted to the state," and that local governments may not "prohibit mobile food dispensing vehicles . . . from operating within the entirety of the entity's jurisdiction." Fla. Stat. § 509.102(2)(a) (2024) (emphasis added). The Lee County ordinance does not impose a separate "license, registration, permit, or fee" on Defendant's vessel; rather, it conditions vending on County park property on a written permit from the Board of County Commissioners or its designee. And the ordinance plainly does not prohibit mobile food dispensing throughout the entirety of Lee County—Defendant remains free to operate anywhere outside the County park system. The selective regulation of vending on park property is precisely the type of localized, location-specific regulation that § 509.102 leaves intact. See Op. Att'y Gen. Fla. 2014-09 (preemption permits "limited new regulation" by local government so long as the operation is not prohibited entity-wide).

C.   Defendant's State License Provides No Substantive Defense.

        Defendant's DBPR Mobile Food Dispensing license, Def. Ex. 4, authorizes him to prepare and sell food consistent with State sanitation standards. It does not authorize him to commandeer the dry sand of a County park for commercial purposes without a vending permit. By analogy, a state-licensed restaurateur may not open a brick-and-mortar restaurant on County park land merely because he holds a state license; nor may a state-licensed liquor distributor sell from a county-owned playground. State licensure addresses food safety; the County ordinance addresses where—on County land—vending may occur. The two operate in distinct regulatory spheres and do not conflict.

III. DEFENDANT HAS NOT ESTABLISHED EQUITABLE ESTOPPEL.

        Defendant's third argument—that "[D]efendant reasonably relied on official County guidance"—fails as a matter of law. Mot. to Dismiss at 2.

        Equitable estoppel against a governmental entity applies "only in rare instances and under exceptional circumstances." Council Bros., Inc. v. City of Tallahassee, 634 So. 2d 264, 266 (Fla. 1st DCA 1994) (quoting N. Am. Co. v. Green, 120 So. 2d 603, 610 (Fla. 1959)). The party invoking the doctrine must establish: "(1) a representation as to a material fact that is contrary to a later-asserted position; (2) reliance on that representation; and (3) a change in position detrimental to the party claiming estoppel, caused by the representation and reliance thereon." Id. (quoting State Dep't of Revenue v. Anderson, 403 So. 2d 397, 400 (Fla. 1981)). Against the government, the movant must additionally show "affirmative conduct by the government which goes beyond mere negligence," "serious injustice" if estoppel is denied, and that "application of estoppel will not unduly harm the public interest." Id. at 267 (citing Alachua County v. Cheshire, 603 So. 2d 1334, 1337 (Fla. 1st DCA 1992)).

        Defendant has not satisfied a single element. He has not identified any County official, any date, any communication, any subject-matter, or any factual representation. He has produced no document evidencing the alleged "guidance." He has not shown any change in position taken in detrimental reliance. And the alleged "guidance"—that "no additional county license was required" because of operation "below the ordinary high-water mark"—would be a statement of law, not fact, and "as a general rule, estoppel will not apply to mistaken statements of the law." Council Bros., 634 So. 2d at 266; Anderson, 403 So. 2d at 400.

        Most damaging, the record affirmatively negates good-faith reliance: Ranger Coyle testified—without contradiction—that Defendant "had been warned several times" by her before the citing event "not to do this, just not on county property." Tr. 15:21–23. A vendor who has been repeatedly warned by the County's law-enforcement officer cannot simultaneously claim he reasonably believed the County had blessed his conduct.

        Finally, applying estoppel here would unduly harm the public interest in orderly enforcement of park ordinances. See Council Bros., 634 So. 2d at 267. Estoppel cannot create rights inconsistent with the law, and certainly cannot be invoked to license future violations of a duly-enacted ordinance.

                                       CONCLUSION

        For the foregoing reasons, the County respectfully requests that this Court (i) deny Defendant's Motion to Dismiss in its entirety, (ii) reinstate the citation under Lee County Ordinance No. 18-12, § 4.9, and (iii) proceed to adjudication on the merits.

Exhibit D — Defendant's Exhibit 1 (aerial photograph of Dog Beach Park).
Exhibit E — Defendant's Exhibit 2 (photograph of vessel location, April 10, 2025).
Exhibit F — Defendant's Exhibit 4 (DBPR Mobile Food Dispensing License No. MFD4651374).

      PLAINTIFF'S AMENDED RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO DEFENDANT'S MOTION TO DISMISS

        Plaintiff, the State of Florida (acting through the Office of the Lee County Attorney), files this Amended Response, which supersedes the Response filed September 12, 2025 only as to the matters expressly amended below, and incorporates by reference all argument from that Response not amended herein. The amendments are made to introduce, and address the evidentiary significance of, three documents that came into the County's possession after September 7, 2025: (i) the 2001 Lease Agreement between Lee County and the Florida Department of Environmental Protection ("FDEP Lease"); (ii) the certified GIS Aerial Map of Dog Beach Park prepared by Lee County Geographical Information Systems Division ("GIS Map"); and (iii) screenshot images of Defendant's commercial website ("Website Screenshots"). Each is admissible and decisively undermines the premises of the Motion to Dismiss.

                                  AMENDED ARGUMENT

I.   THE FDEP LEASE CONFIRMS THAT DOG BEACH WAS DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED FROM THE STATE-PARK LEASE AND REMAINS UNDER LEE COUNTY'S DIRECT JURISDICTION.

A.   Evidentiary Significance.

        On June 12, 2001, Lee County executed a fifty-year lease with FDEP, Division of Recreation and Parks, for the operation of Carl Johnson Park as a unit of the Florida State Park System under the management of Lovers Key State Park. FDEP Lease, recitals & §§ 1, 3 (Pl.'s Am. Ex. H). The recitals make clear that the parties expressly "remove[d] the area described in Exhibit B [of the Lease] to allow establishment of Dog Beach." Id. (third "WHEREAS" clause). The fourth recital confirms: "WHEREAS, the area identified as Dog Beach will be an area where citizens can allow their dogs to roam leash free." Id. The Lease's body, § 1 ("DESCRIPTION OF PARK"), then limits the leasehold strictly "to those areas specifically identified in attached Exhibit A" — i.e., the area encompassed by Carl Johnson Park, not Dog Beach.

        The legal consequence is dispositive of Defendant's first argument. Dog Beach Park is County-owned land that the County deliberately retained from the State-park lease and continues to manage directly through the Lee County Department of Parks and Recreation. It is not "State property" for purposes of Defendant's preemption theory; it is County park property, fully subject to Lee County Ordinance No. 18-12, § 4.9. Whatever doctrinal force Stop the Beach Renourishment, Inc. v. Florida Department of Environmental Protection, 560 U.S. 702 (2010), or Broward v. Mabry, 58 Fla. 398, 50 So. 826 (Fla. 1909), might have over true sovereignty submerged lands, neither speaks to the County's primary, fee-owner authority over the upland park sand of Dog Beach.

B.   Admissibility.

        The FDEP Lease is admissible. As an executed agreement of a Florida county political subdivision and a State agency, the Lease is a public record kept by both parties in the regular course of governmental administration. It is admissible under the public-records exception to the hearsay rule, Fla. Stat. § 90.803(8) (2024), and is self-authenticating as an "official document" of a Florida political subdivision and a State agency, Fla. Stat. § 90.902(1)–(2), (4) (2024). To the extent any portion of the Lease is offered for the truth of its descriptive recitals concerning the metes and bounds of the leasehold and the exclusion of Dog Beach, those statements are operative legal terms (verbal acts) defining the scope of the lease and are not hearsay at all. See Charles W. Ehrhardt, Florida Evidence § 801.6 (2024 ed.). The original or a duplicate is sufficient under Fla. Stat. § 90.953 (2024).

II.  THE GIS AERIAL MAP CONCLUSIVELY SHOWS THAT THE LOCATION OF DEFENDANT'S VENDING WAS WITHIN THE OFFICIAL BOUNDARIES OF DOG BEACH PARK.

A.   Evidentiary Significance.

        The GIS Map, captioned "Lee County Parks & Recreation, Dog Beach Park, 14436 Bonita Beach Causeway," is a current aerial overlay of the Park's boundary, prepared by the Lee County Geographical Information Systems Division on August 25, 2025, from January–February 2025 aerial photography. GIS Map, p. 1 (Pl.'s Am. Ex. I). The bounded "current use area" depicted in red includes both the dry-sand peninsula on which Defendant's vessel grounded and the immediately adjacent foreshore area used by patrons to approach the vessel. When compared to Defendant's own Exhibit 2 (a photograph showing the vessel's location on April 10, 2025), the GIS Map confirms that Defendant's vending occurred squarely within the boundary of Dog Beach Park.

        The map also corrects the deficiency the Court identified at the June 25, 2025 hearing. At that hearing, the Court sustained Defendant's objection to the Ranger's prior, unauthenticated boundary map because the witness "[could] not testify" to "who creates the line to indicate that it is actually the property line." Tr. 15:3–6. The newly-produced GIS Map cures that foundational defect: it is accompanied by a sworn declaration of authentication from Amy Hoyt, GIS Manager and the records custodian for the Lee County GIS Division, executed under penalty of perjury and complying with Fla. Stat. §§ 90.803(6) and 90.902(11) (2024). GIS Map, p. 2 (Hoyt Decl.).

B.   Admissibility.

        The GIS Map is admissible on three independent grounds. First, it is an authenticated business record under Fla. Stat. § 90.803(6) (2024), with the statutory foundational requirements certified by the records custodian's sworn declaration as authorized by Fla. Stat. § 90.902(11) (2024). Hoyt Decl. (certifying that the record was made at or near the time of the events from information by a person with knowledge, was kept in the course of regularly conducted activity, and was made in the ordinary course of that activity). Second, it is a public record admissible under Fla. Stat. § 90.803(8) (2024), as a record of activities of a public office (the County's GIS Division), prepared in the regular performance of duty. Third, the Map is a self-authenticating "[c]opy of an official public record . . . certified as correct by the custodian" under Fla. Stat. § 90.902(4) (2024).

        The Map is plainly relevant: it has the tendency to make a fact of consequence — whether Defendant operated within the boundary of Dog Beach Park — more probable than it would be without the evidence. See Fla. Stat. § 90.401 (2024); Fla. Stat. § 90.402 (2024). To the extent the Court treats the depicted boundary as an opinion of the GIS Division, it is admissible non-expert opinion of the public agency entrusted by Lee County with cartographic responsibility. The Map is thus in evidence both for the fact of the boundary and as circumstantial evidence that Defendant's documented operational location fell within the Park.

III. DEFENDANT'S OWN COMMERCIAL WEBSITE IS A PARTY ADMISSION THAT THE OPERATION IS A BEACH-DIRECTED VENDING BUSINESS — NOT MERE PRESENCE IN NAVIGABLE WATERS.

A.   Evidentiary Significance.

        The Website Screenshots establish, in Defendant's own words and images, that Defendant's enterprise is a beach-vending business deliberately marketed as "FOOD BOAT: NAUTI GIRL BAD BOUY BBQ AT THE BEACH"; described as "the perfect spot for beach dining"; and advertised as an "incredible BBQ food truck" that "brings the flavors of Big Hickory directly to your plate." Website Screenshots at 1 (Pl.'s Am. Ex. J). The site features images of the vessel itself bearing Florida vessel registration "FL 2463 MM" and the distinctive promotional legend "BRINGING THE BACKYARD BBQ TO YOU!", and lists a menu with priced items (e.g., "Pulled Pork Sanwich [sic] $12," "Smoked Mac n Brisket $20"). Id. at 1, 3, 4. A directional Google Maps printout shows routing terminating at "Bonita Beach Dog Park, 8800 Estero Blvd." Id. at 13.

        These admissions are dispositive of the Motion's central characterization of Defendant's conduct. Defendant cast himself in the Motion to Dismiss as merely operating "in navigable waters adjacent to Dog Beach . . . below the ordinary high-water mark." Mot. to Dismiss ¶ 2. His own marketing tells a different story: he holds himself out as a "food truck" that vends "AT THE BEACH" — that is, at a County park — and routes his patrons to "Bonita Beach Dog Park." This is the very vending activity the County ordinance regulates, and Defendant's website is a contemporaneous, repeated, voluntary admission of it. See Lee County Ordinance No. 18-12, § 4.9.

        The Website Screenshots also rebut Defendant's third argument — equitable reliance on alleged County "guidance" that no permit was required. A vendor who openly markets himself as a beach-side food truck cannot credibly claim to have been ignorant that the conduct sat within the local park-vending ordinance's scope.

B.   Admissibility.

        The Website Screenshots are admissible as party-opponent admissions under Fla. Stat. § 90.803(18)(a)–(b) (2024). They consist of statements made by Defendant himself (or persons authorized by him to speak for his business) in either an individual or representative capacity, or, at minimum, statements that Defendant has manifested an adoption or belief in by publishing them on the website operated to advertise his own business. Fla. Stat. § 90.803(18)(a)–(c) (2024). Statements falling within § 90.803(18) are not hearsay and do not require any further hearsay exception.

        The screenshots are authenticable under Fla. Stat. § 90.901 (2024) by the testimony of Ranger Coyle (or other County witness who personally accessed and printed the website), who can identify the date of capture and the URL of capture, see, e.g., Smith v. State, 250 So. 3d 819, 822 (Fla. 4th DCA 2018), or by reliance on the "appearance, contents, substance, internal patterns, or other distinctive characteristics, taken in conjunction with circumstances," Fla. Stat. § 90.901; see also Lamb v. State, 246 So. 3d 400, 410 (Fla. 4th DCA 2018) (electronic evidence may be authenticated by distinctive characteristics). The screenshots prominently and repeatedly depict the trade name "Nauti Girl Bad Bouy BBQ," the distinctive logo of Defendant's enterprise, and the vessel registration "FL 2463 MM" — all of which corroborate that the website is Defendant's. Cf. State v. Lumarque, 44 So. 3d 171, 173 (Fla. 3d DCA 2010) (electronic evidence may be authenticated through distinctive characteristics).

        The Court should consider Defendant's website both as substantive evidence that vending was directed at and from Dog Beach Park, and as impeachment of any contrary representation Defendant may seek to make at the rehearing.

                              REINCORPORATED ARGUMENT

        The County reincorporates by reference all argument and authority set forth in its September 12, 2025 Response in Opposition to Defendant's Motion to Dismiss, including the discussion of: (i) the unrebutted record evidence that Defendant's vessel was partially grounded on the dry sand of Dog Beach Park, Tr. 8:18–19, 12:4–9, 21:23–25; (ii) Lee County's home-rule authority under Article VIII, § 1(f) of the Florida Constitution and Florida Statutes § 125.01(1)(h), (t) (2024); (iii) the limited scope of state-law preemption under Fla. Stat. §§ 509.032(7) and 509.102(2)(a) (2024); and (iv) the demanding standard for equitable estoppel against a governmental entity, Council Bros., Inc. v. City of Tallahassee, 634 So. 2d 264, 266–67 (Fla. 1st DCA 1994); State Dep't of Revenue v. Anderson, 403 So. 2d 397, 400 (Fla. 1981).

                                       CONCLUSION

        The newly-discovered FDEP Lease establishes that Dog Beach Park is County land excluded from any State-park leasehold; the certified GIS Map establishes that Defendant operated within the official boundary of that County park; and Defendant's own Website Screenshots establish that the operation was — in Defendant's own marketing words — a "FOOD BOAT . . . AT THE BEACH" vending business. Each of the three pillars of the Motion to Dismiss collapses under this record. The County respectfully requests that the Court (i) deny the Motion to Dismiss in its entirety, (ii) reinstate the citation under Lee County Ordinance No. 18-12, § 4.9, and (iii) proceed to adjudication on the merits at the September 17, 2025 hearing.

The Amended Response expressly discusses the website screenshots as newly discovered evidence and specifically notes that a Google Maps directional printout routes patrons to “Bonita Beach Dog Park, 8800 Estero Blvd.” It uses that fact to argue Defendant’s operation was “AT THE BEACH” and “at a County park,” which is the substance of the criterion. While the phrase “knowingly operating within a county park” is not quoted verbatim, the response clearly states the Google map link/directions on Defendant’s website are evidence that the vending operation was directed to a county park and thus was within County park property. That satisfies the criterion in context.

The criterion requires that the Amended Response specifically state that the Website document is admissible as a web mapping service under Fla. Stat. § 90.2035(1)(a). In the provided answer, the Website Screenshots are instead discussed as party-opponent admissions under Fla. Stat. § 90.803(18) and as electronically authenticable evidence. There is no statement in the required context that the Website document itself is admissible as a web mapping service under § 90.2035(1)(a). Therefore, the criterion is not satisfied.

The answer includes a clearly labeled section titled “EXHIBIT LIST” within the Amended Response to the Defendant’s Motion to Dismiss (Assignment 3), and it lists multiple exhibits (A through J). This satisfies the criterion, which only asks whether an exhibit list is identified in the amended response.

The criterion asks whether the Amended Response includes a Certificate of Service. In the provided answer, Assignment 3 ends with a clearly labeled "CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE" section, which states the filing date, method of service, and recipients. This directly satisfies the criterion in the correct context.

   Highlights:
  - - Sovereign Submerged Lands (SSL) are those lands including but not limited to, tidal lands, islands, sand bars, shallow banks, and lands waterward of the ordinary or mean high water line, beneath navigable fresh water or beneath tidally-influenced waters, which the State of Florida acquired title to on March 3, 1845, by virtue of statehood, and which have not been heretofore conveyed or alienated. (18-21.003, Florida Administrative Code)
[...]
- Prior to the merger into the Department of Environmental Protection (DEP), the Department of Environmental
[...]
had regulatory jurisdiction over certain activities affecting
[...]
The following explains the current proprietary and regulatory functions of DEP's Submerged Lands and Environmental Resource Permitting.
[...]
- Regulatory authority allows an entity of the government, such as DEP, to limit certain activities on property, as well as on publicly owned lands, to some specific degree for the greater public good. DEP, in its regulatory capacity, is required by acts of the Florida Legislature, to protect the natural resources of the state, such as air, water and wildlife, to insure that these resources will be healthy and abundant for present and future generations. DEP's Submerged Lands and Environmental Resources Coordination program reviews applications for proposed works in wetlands and other surface waters, as well as works in uplands that can affect water quality and quantity, to ensure compliance with the Florida Administrative Code and Florida Statutes.
[...]
- Proprietary authority: The State Legislature designated the Governor and Cabinet as the Board of Trustees of the Internal Improvement Trust Fund of the State of Florida (Board of Trustees) in 1845. The Board of Trustees were given proprietary (ownership) authority over sovereign submerged lands (SSL) and their uses, and were held responsible for insuring the lands and the associated aquatic resources remained healthy and in abundance for present and future generations. All tidally influenced waters to the mean high water line and navigable fresh waterbodies to the ordinary high water line in existence when Florida became a state in 1845 are considered sovereign. In accordance with the Constitution of the State of Florida, these lands are held in trust by the state for all the people.
[...]
- The Florida Department of Environmental Protection, in addition to its regulatory capacity, acts as the staff to the Board of Trustees in the review of proposed uses of sovereign submerged lands (SSL). Projects proposing to conduct an activity in waters that are not SSL are required to meet regulatory standards only. A proposed activity located on SSL may be required to meet both regulatory and proprietary requirements as found in the Florida Statutes and Florida Administrative Code.
[...]
The first amendment, section 18-21.00401, F.A.C., known as the linkage rule, links the review and issuance (or denial) of a proprietary authorization to use sovereign submerged lands (SSL) with the review and issuance (or denial) of a regulatory authorization (an environmental resource permit, a wetland resource permit (grandfathered) or a joint coastal permit). Linkage eliminates situations where a regulatory permit is granted for an activity that does not qualify for a proprietary authorization, or vice versa.
[...]
The second amendment, section 18-21.0051, F.A.C., known as the delegation rule, gives the decision-making authority of the Board of Trustees, for certain* actions regarding the use of sovereign submerged lands, to the Department and to the above cited water management districts. The delegation shortens the time and reduces the number of levels of review for the proprietary decision-making process. The delegation also facilitates the concurrent processing of the linked applications (proprietary and regulatory) by the Department and the Districts, as described previously.

• Derived from early Roman civil law, the “negative community”

• Res communes – things common to all or res nullius – things 
owned by no one – objects in the “negative community” are 
not considered “property” of any one person.

THE EQUAL FOOTING DOCTRINE – TITLE 
GOES TO FLORIDA
• Following the American Revolution, the original 13 colonies won their 
independence and achieved sovereignty – thus, each held sovereign 
ownership to lands under the navigable waters and carried those 
rights with them when they joined the Union.
• Upon acquisition of territory by the United States, title to these lands 
passed to the U.S.
• Following adoption of the Constitution, any new state’s admission 
into the Union must be on “equal footing” with the original 13 states, 
and the new state enters possessing the same rights as the original 
states.

SECTION 01 Powers and duties.

 F.S. 125.01

125.01 Powers and duties.—

(1) The legislative and governing body of a county shall have the power to carry on county government. To the extent not inconsistent with general or special law, this power includes, but is not restricted to, the power to:

(a) Adopt its own rules of procedure, select its officers, and set the time and place of its official meetings.

(b) Provide for the prosecution and defense of legal causes in behalf of the county or state and retain counsel and set their compensation.

(c) Provide and maintain county buildings.

(d) Provide fire protection, including the enforcement of the Florida Fire Prevention Code, as provided in ss. 633.206 and 633.208, and adopt and enforce local technical amendments to the Florida Fire Prevention Code as provided in those sections and pursuant to s. 633.202.

(e) Provide hospitals, ambulance service, and health and welfare programs.

(f) Provide parks, preserves, playgrounds, recreation areas, libraries, museums, historical commissions, and other recreation and cultural facilities and programs.

(g) Prepare and enforce comprehensive plans for the development of the county.

(h) Establish, coordinate, and enforce zoning and such business regulations as are necessary for the protection of the public.

(i) Adopt, by reference or in full, and enforce housing and related technical codes and regulations.

(j) Establish and administer programs of housing, slum clearance, community redevelopment, conservation, flood and beach erosion control, air pollution control, and navigation and drainage and cooperate with governmental agencies and private enterprises in the development and operation of such programs.

(k)1. Provide and regulate waste and sewage collection and disposal, water and alternative water supplies, including, but not limited to, reclaimed water and water from aquifer storage and recovery and desalination systems, and conservation programs.

2. The governing body of a county may require that any person within the county demonstrate the existence of some arrangement or contract by which such person will dispose of solid waste in a manner consistent with county ordinance or state or federal law.    Highlights:
  - Practitioners know that civil and appellate rules contemplate motions for rehearing. But what is the difference between the two rules? Simply put, one leaves the door open for new arguments while the other keeps it shut.
[...]
Rule 1.530(a): “on a motion for rehearing of matters heard without a jury, including summary judgments, the court may open the judgment if one has been entered, take additional testimony, and enter a new judgment.”
[...]
Rule 9.330(a): “state with particularity the points of law or fact that, in the opinion of the movant, the court has overlooked or misapprehended in its decision, and shall not present issues not previously raised in the proceeding.”
[...]
While a Rule 1.530 motion is your last chance to preserve issues for appeal and may raise new arguments, Rule 9.330 motions are limited to mistakes or oversights by the appellate court based on the issues already raised. As explained in the procedurally nuanced decision in Fitchner v. Lifesouth Community, 88 So. 3d 269 (Fla. 1st DCA 2012), Rule 1.530 is necessarily broader by procedural design.
[...]
In Fitchner, the appellate court considered a new argument raised in plaintiff’s 1.530 rehearing motion that followed the dismissal of its complaint. Although the trial court acknowledged the new argument established the dismissal was based on a statute that did not even apply, it denied the motion for rehearing after concluding the new argument was untimely. Observing trial courts have the discretion to ignore new arguments, the appellate court found the trial court’s ruling was “an unnecessary triumph of procedure over substance” and therefore an abuse of discretion. Criticizing the trial court’s failure to employ simple judicial economy to remedy the situation, the appellate court reversed the dismissal.
[...]
Ultimately, Rule 9.330 is as limited as Rule 1.530 is open-ended. So while Rule 1.530 motions are expectedly commonplace, Rule 9.330 motions should be employed under very limited circumstances – and with extreme caution. Appellate courts have long since been frustrated with the perceived frequency of 9.330 motions, one court declaring such motions seemed “to occupy a singular status of abuse” in our legal system. Lawyers Title Insurance Corp., v. Reitzes, 631 So. 2d 110 (Fla. 4th DCA 1993). In those instances where the motion is viewed as simply bemoaning “the bottomless depth of displeasure” of an unsuccessful appeal in “open defiance of Rule 9.330,” sanctions may follow. McDonnell v. Sanford Airport Authority, 2015 WL 2260504 (Fla. 5th DCA 2015).
[...]
Rule 1.530 may serve as a safety net for an overlooked argument, but as Fitchner emphasized, a trial has the discretion to ignore it. If that happens, demonstrating the trial court abused its discretion may prove out of reach on appeal. Likewise, an ill-conceived Rule 9.330 motion may be branded “meritless and insulting” and result in an invitation to show cause why sanctions should not be imposed.
[...]
But of course there is an exception – but only in exceptionally rare instances. When reviewing a Rule 9.330 motion for rehearing, an appellate court may exercise its discretion to consider a new argument or information in effort to avoid fundamental error.

10. When a Motion for Rehearing Can Blow Your Appeal Deadline: Shutts & Bowen LLP
   URL: https://www.shutts.com/business-and-legal-insights/rehearing-appeal-deadline
   Highlights:
  - Rule 1.530(a) of the Florida Rules of Civil Procedure authorizes a motion for rehearing directed to a final order entered after a summary disposition or bench trial. There are benefits to filing a motion for rehearing; however, practitioners should keep in mind the risk in filing an untimely motion and how it affects the appeal process.
[...]
(a) Jury and Non-Jury Actions. A new trial may be granted to all or any of the parties and on all or a part of the issues. On a motion for rehearing of matters heard without a jury, including summary judgments, the court may open the judgment if one has been entered, take additional testimony, and enter a new judgment.
[...]
The purpose of such a motion is to provide the trial court an opportunity to correct an error if it is convinced it has erred. As practitioners know, filing a motion for rehearing generally suspends rendition (tolls the time for filing an appeal) of a final judgment until the trial court disposes of the rehearing motion. Fla. R. App. P. 9.020(i).
[...]
But, can filing a motion for rehearing blow a party’s right to appeal? Yes! Under Rule 9.020(i), rendition of a final order is suspended when “there has been filed in the lower tribunal an authorized and timely” motion for rehearing. Filing an untimely or unauthorized rehearing motion does not toll the time to file a notice of appeal. In determining whether a motion for rehearing will toll the time for filing a notice of appeal, it is critical to make sure that the motion is both authorized and timely.
[...]
1. Late motion for rehearing of final judgment: Rule 1.530(b) requires the rehearing motion to be served not later than 15 days after the date of filing of the judgment. So a motion for rehearing served 17 days after the date the judgment is filed is untimely. Assume the trial court denies the untimely motion 31 days after the judgment was entered and the losing party files a notice of appeal the next day. In that scenario, the appellate court lacks jurisdiction to review the final judgment and the appeal will be dismissed. See, MCB Oil Co. v. City of Gainesville, 932 So. 2d 504 (Fla. 1st DCA 2006). In that same scenario, however, a notice of appeal of the judgment would be timely so long as the notice was filed within thirty days of the date the judgment was filed.
[...]
2. Motion for rehearing directed to non-final order: Rule 9.130 authorizes interlocutory review of specified non-final orders (e.g., orders determining venue; injunctive relief; class certification; entitlement to arbitration). Since Rule 1.530 only authorizes rehearing motions directed to final orders, motions for rehearing are not “authorized” as to non-final orders listed in Rule 9.130 and will not toll the time to file a notice of appeal. See, Princess Cruises, Inc. v. Edwards, 611 So. 2d 598 (Fla. 2d DCA 1993). The same principle applies in original proceedings involving non-final orders. Thus, for example, a party who intends to petition for certiorari as to an order compelling discovery should not move for rehearing. An untimely 9.130 appeal or petition for certiorari will be dismissed.

1. Enforcement of ordinance on waterway | My Florida Legal
   URL: https://www.myfloridalegal.com/ag-opinions/enforcement-of-ordinance-on-waterway
   Highlights:
  - MUNICIPALITIES--MAY ENFORCE MUNICIPAL ORDINANCES ON WATERWAYS WITHIN THEIR JURISDICTION To: Roger H. Wilson, Representative, 60th District, Seminole Prepared by: Andrew W. Lindsey, Assistant Attorney General QUESTION: What authority do municipal officers have to enforce municipal ordinances dealing with water safety? SUMMARY: Municipal officers may enforce restricted areas and local ordinances on waterways within their jurisdiction, as provided in Ch. 371, F. S. Said enforcement may be by fresh pursuit in accordance with s. 901.25, F. S. There are two methods whereby a municipality or a county may restrict traffic on the waterways within their jurisdiction. Section 371.522, F. S., provides a method whereby the governing body of the county or municipality may establish a restricted area by petitioning the Division of Marine Resources of the Department of Natural Resources. Said division, after an investigation, may then establish the requested restricted area when it determines a safety hazard exists. Section 371.67, F. S., then provides for enforcement of the above set out restricted area. Section 371.59, F. S., provides that ordinances or local laws may be enacted to regulate the operation of any vessel upon the waterways within the jurisdiction of the body enacting either the ordinance or the local law so long as said ordinance or local law is not in conflict with provisions of Ch. 371, F. S. Section 371.59 further provides ordinances or local laws may not attempt to regulate traffic on the Florida Intracoastal Waterway. Section 371.68, F. S., provides the penalty for violation of Ch. 371, F. S., said penalty being a second degree misdemeanor, which would authorize law enforcement officers to make arrest, as provided in s. 901.15(1), F. S., which states: "901.15 When arrest by officer without warrant is lawful. -- A peace officer may arrest a person without a warrant when: (1) The person has committed a felony or misdemeanor or violated a municipal ordinance in the presence of the officer. Arrest for the commission of a misdemeanor or violation of a municipal ordinance shall be made immediately or in fresh pursuit." Section 901.25, F. S., further provides for a municipal officer to make a fresh pursuit of a person under certain prescribed conditions, when it states: "901.25 Municipal officer, arrest outside corporate limits in fresh pursuit. -- A police officer of a municipality, when necessary to make an arrest, may make a fresh pursuit of a person from within the municipality to any point in the county in which the municipality is located when the person pursued has violated a city ordinance or committed a misdemeanor within the municipality, or the officer reasonably believes that the person has committed or is committing a felony."

2. CITY OF CORAL GABLES V. TIEN
   URL: https://law.justia.com/cases/florida/third-district-court-of-appeal/2007/3d07-1219.html
   Highlights:
  - the vessel, when moored behind Bared s home, protrudes approximately twenty feet into what Tien considers his space, in the waterway. After asking nicely, in writing, to please move the boat and receiving an unneighborly response, Tien complained to the City Code Enforcement Department who cited Mr. Bared under Section 86-59 of the Coral Gables Code. This section provides: It shall be unlawful for any person to anchor, moor or tie up any boat or craft of any and every nature whatsoever to any waterfront property abutting the waterways and canals within the city, unless he is the owner of the property to which the craft is anchored, moored or tied up or is the lessee of improved property having a dwelling structure thereon, under a written lease from the owner of the fee simple title to 1 See Art. V, §4(b)(3), Fla. Const.; Fla. R. App. P. 9.030(b)(2)(B); City of Deerfield Beach v. Vaillant, 419 So. 2d 624 (Fla. 1982). 2 such property or is the guest in the house of the owner of improved property having a dwelling structure thereon. Code 1958, §7-5; Code 1991, §14-41. Bared would not budge. Instead, he appealed to the Coral Gables Code Enforcement Board. At the hearing before the Board, Tien presented what he considered to be watertight evidence in support of his position: [T]o park a 122-foot boat off 100 feet of waterfront . . . , [y]ou are either going to be 22 feet into one neighbor s space or an aggregate of 22 feet into two neighbors spaces. Bared conceded this point, but countered that the ordinance was inapplicable because this boat is anchored solely to Bared s own property. The City Attorney opined this was the determinative fact in the case, and the Board dismissed the violation. On first tier certiorari, the circuit court appellate division disagreed with the Code Enforcement Board s decision. Conceding the yacht was parked along [Bared s] seawall behind his own home, the appellate court chose to focus on Tien s equally indisputable point that the yacht did extend over behind Tien s seawall . . . as well. The appellate court considered this fact sufficient to award relief to Tien under the ordinance and concluded, [a]ny other interpretation of the statute would result in an absurd result . . . . Bared now seeks to invoke our assistance. We recognize at the outset that the scope of our review at this stage of the proceeding is quite limited. Where, as here, full review of administrative action is 3 given in the circuit court as a matter of right, a litigant is not entitled to a second full review in the district court. City of Deerfield Beach v. Vaillant, 419 So. 2d 624, 626 (Fla. 1982). However, where there has been a violation of a clearly established principle of law resulting in a miscarriage of justice, then we are authorized to reach down and supply relief. Allstate Ins. Co. v. Kaklamanos, 843 So. 2d 885, 888 (Fla. 2003) (citing Ivey v. Allstate Ins. Co., 774 So. 2d 679, 682 (Fla. 2000)). As the court noted in Kaklamanos, clearly established law can derive from a variety of legal sources, including recent controlling case law, rules of court, statutes, and constitutional law. Kaklamanos, 843 So. 2d at 890. To that list, we today add municipal ordinances. Applying Kaklamanos, we conclude it would be a violation of clearly established law and a substantial miscarriage of justice if this mega-yacht was banned from the City of Coral Gables based upon this ordinance. We are compelled to this conclusion based upon a plain reading of the ordinance. Originally adopted in 1958, when Coral Gables had considerably more vacant land within its limits than it has today, the ordinance prohibited the anchoring, mooring, or tying up of any waterfront property abutting the waterways and canals within the city. Although legislative intent is not our polestar, we doubt the city parents of that time were concerned about mega-yachts. WHETHER A MUNICIPALITY HAS THE ABILITY 
TO REGULATE MOORINGS ON UNDERWATER 
LAND OWNED, LEASED OR ADJACENT TO IT? 
A municipality's ability to regulate moorings on underwater land owned, leased or 
adjacent to it is limited by operation of the Florida Statutes. The applicable statute is §327.60 
Fla. Statutes, which reads: 
327.60 Local regulations; limitations. 
(1) The provisions of [chapter 327] and chapter 328 shall govern the operation, 
equipment, and all other matters relating thereto whenever any vessel shall be operated 
upon the waters of this state or when any activity regulated hereby shall take place 
thereon.
[...]
(2) Nothing in this chapter or chapter 328 shall be construed to prevent the adoption of 
any ordinance or local regulation relating to operation of vessels, except that a county 
or municipality shall not enact, continue in effect, or enforce any ordinance or local 
regulation: 
(a) Establishing a vessel or associated equipment performance or other safety 
standard, imposing a requirement for associated equipment, or regulating the 
carrying or use of marine safety articles;
[...]
(3) Nothing in this section shall be construed to prohibit local governmental authorities 
from the enactment or enforcement of regulations which prohibit or restrict the mooring 
or anchoring of :floating structures or live-aboard vessels within their jurisdictions or of 
any vessels within the marked boundaries of mooring fields permitted as provided in s. 
327.40. However, local governmental authorities are prohibited from regulating the 
anchoring outside of such mooring fields of vessels other than live-aboard vessels as 
defined ins. 327.02. Emphasis added 
The above-referenced statute provides that a municipality may regulate mooring by 
establishing marked mooring fields in accordance with state law. This means that a 
municipality may designate and mark a certain area of water as a "mooring field." The 
municipality must seek and obtain approval from the State of Florida before it may place any 
markers designating the boundaries of the mooring field. Once the markers are properly put 
into place the municipality may take enforcement action against any vessel that does not have 
permission to anchor in the mooring field. 
A municipality may not, however, regulate the mooring of vessels outside the marked 
mooring fields. This means that those boaters who are unwilling to pay for moorings are still 
allowed to anchor outside the marked boundaries of mooring fields. 
Conclusion 
The City's authority to regulate the mooring of vessels in or upon the waters 
owned or leased by the City is limited to areas designated as mooring fields that have been 
properly marked according to the provisions of Florida law. The City does not have the 
authority to regulate the mooring of vessels outside of the designated mooring fields.

I must emphasize at the outset that this opinion is strictly limited to a consideration of a municipality's authority to regulate vessels and is not to be considered a comment on ownership of artificial waterbodies or regulation of activities other than those in Ch. 327, F.S.[1] Section 327.02(28), F.S., defining the phrase "[w]aters of this state" for purposes of regulation, provides that: "'Waters of this state' means any navigable waters of the United States within the territorial limits of this state, and the marginal sea adjacent to this state and the high seas when navigated as a part of a journey or ride to or from the shore of this state, and all the inland lakes, rivers, and canals under the jurisdiction of this state." SUMMARY: The Town of Melbourne Beach does not have lawful authority to enact an ordinance regulating the taking of fish from a manmade canal within its corporate limits. The Town of Melbourne Beach is without authority to regulate water traffic on an artificially created body of water which has remained private property. The first question is answered in the negative. In describing the need for the opinion, your letter refers to commercial fishermen blocking the canals with nets at times so that boats of others are not able to use the canals. This, together with knowledge of the location of Melbourne Beach, causes me to assume that the water which occupied the manmade canals when dug is salt water from the Atlantic Ocean. Albeit, the question will be answered first assuming the water in the manmade canals is salt water and then answered assuming the water in question is fresh water. For clarification of the question it is well to remember at this point that the Legislature in 1973, pursuant to Art. VIII, s. 2(b), State Const., gave municipalities home rule powers by Ch. 73-129, Laws of Florida, and designated such powers "Municipal Home Rule Powers Act" which appears as Ch. 166, F. S. Section 166.021(1) and (3)(c), provides as follows: "(1) As provided in article VIII, section 2(b) of the state constitution, municipalities shall have the governmental, corporate, and proprietary powers to enable them to conduct municipal government, perform municipal functions, and render municipal services, and may exercise any power for municipal purposes, except when expressly prohibited by law. * * * * * (3)(c) Any subject expressly preempted to state or county government by the constitution or by general law; . . . ." The above-referenced statute provides that a municipality may regulate mooring by 
establishing marked mooring fields in accordance with state law. This means that a 
municipality may designate and mark a certain area of water as a "mooring field." The 
municipality must seek and obtain approval from the State of Florida before it may place any 
markers designating the boundaries of the mooring field. Once the markers are properly put 
into place the municipality may take enforcement action against any vessel that does not have 
permission to anchor in the mooring field. 
A municipality may not, however, regulate the mooring of vessels outside the marked 
mooring fields. This means that those boaters who are unwilling to pay for moorings are still 
allowed to anchor outside the marked boundaries of mooring fields. 
Conclusion 
The City's authority to regulate the mooring of vessels in or upon the waters 
owned or leased by the City is limited to areas designated as mooring fields that have been 
properly marked according to the provisions of Florida law. The City does not have the 
authority to regulate the mooring of vessels outside of the designated mooring fields.

Dear Mr. Denhardt: As the attorney for the City of Treasure Island, you ask substantially the following question: May a municipality enact and enforce ordinances to prohibit the unauthorized trespass upon, or the unauthorized mooring of a boat to, a privately-owned dock located over state-owned submerged lands within the corporate limits of the municipality, when the property owner's right to such dock is derived through riparian or littoral property rights? In sum: A municipality may enact and enforce an ordinance to prohibit the unauthorized trespass upon or the unauthorized mooring of a boat to a privately-owned dock located over state-owned submerged lands, within the city's corporate limits, consistent with the general laws applicable to trespass. The general legal principle applicable to your inquiry is that a municipality has civil and criminal jurisdiction over property within its corporate boundaries and may regulate and restrict certain activities reasonably calculated to protect the public health, safety, and welfare.[1] The power of a municipality to regulate, however, is subject to the state's paramount power to regulate and control the use of its sovereign lands. To the extent that any such regulation has been preempted by the state or is inconsistent with general law or with regulations adopted by the state, any attempted municipal regulation would be invalid.[2] Application of a trespass statute or ordinance to a private dock would appear to depend upon the nature of the ownership of such property. It has been recognized that riparian owners have historically been entitled to greater rights in relation to the waters that border their land than enjoyed by the public generally.[3] As riparian owners, they have the exclusive right of access over their own property to the water. The public has no right to cross the riparian owner's private property to reach the navigable waters.[4] Subject to applicable regulations and permitting procedures, the owner of riparian property may construct and maintain a wharf, dock, or pier from his or her land to the navigable portion of adjoining waters.[5] This entitlement, however, is subject to the paramount rights of the public and the private rights of other riparian landowners.[6] The Supreme Court of Florida in several cases has found this entitlement to be a common law right that accompanies the ownership of the riparian property.[7] Thus, riparian property owners in Florida have a qualified right to build docks or "wharf out" to navigable water and have exclusive rights to use their private property. It would appear, therefore, that a dock or wharf constructed by the riparian owner with the consent of the state operates as an extension of the riparian owner's private property interest that may be protected under the laws of this state. Section 810.09(1), Florida Statutes, provides: "Whoever, without being authorized, licensed, or invited, willfully enters upon or remains in any property other than a structure or conveyance as to which notice against entering or remaining is given, either by actual communication to the offender or by posting, fencing, or cultivation as described in s. 810.011, commits the offense of trespass on property other than a structure or conveyance."[8] In the absence of actual notice being given to an individual who is on or moored to a private dock without permission, the property must either be posted, fenced or under cultivation in order to provide the necessary element of notice. Of these three methods of notice, posting and fencing lend themselves more readily in applying the trespass statute to a private wharf or dock. Is the City of Clearwater empowered to repeal an exemption relating to riparian rights from an ordinance prohibiting boat traffic within 300 feet of designated public beaches? 2. If the answer to Question 1 is in the affirmative, could the city be subject to liability for compensation for the taking of an abutting property owner's riparian rights if such an exemption were repealed? Questions one and two are interrelated and will be answered together. Your letter states that the City of Clearwater has enacted an ordinance prohibiting boat traffic within 300 feet of certain designated public beaches. The purpose of this regulation is to protect the safety and health of swimmers within that area. An ordinance recognizing the "riparian rights" of abutting property owners constitutes an exemption to the general prohibition of boat traffic within 300 feet of designated public beaches. Property owners along these designated beaches have been leasing their properties for commercial ventures. Among the commercial uses to which such property has been put is for the launching of paddle boats and other vessels for tourists which, in order to get to open water, must travel through the prohibited zone. The City of Clearwater is concerned that the exemption for "riparian rights" permits the frequent launching and mooring of vessels through the protected area, thereby effectively defeating the purpose of the ordinance and is therefore considering repealing the ordinance. Repeal of the ordinance recognizing the exemption for "riparian rights" would be accomplished by enactment of a municipal ordinance to that effect. For purposes of exactness it should be noted that although the terms are often used interchangeably and the rights they entail are the same, "riparian rights" are those which are connected with or follow the ownership of banks and streams and rivers while the rights associated with lands bordering on tidewaters are "littoral rights." See Johnson v. McCowen, 348 So.2d 357, 360 (1 D.C.A. Fla., 1977); Gillilan v. Knighton, 420 So.2d 924, 925 (2 D.C.A. Fla., 1982). I would note, however, that even the courts in Florida use such terms interchangeably and s. 197.228, F.S., which defines riparian rights does not distinguish between different types of navigable waters.
